title: Four Nights of a Dreamer (1971)
subtitle: Quatre nuits d’un rêveur
content:
*Originally watched May 24, 2026*

(wip)

The richness of Dostoyevsky's White Nights lies in the delusional passion of its narrator’s expressive monologues. So, it's interesting that Robert Bresson, a director known for his aversion to performed emotion, decided to adapt a novella that lives in what he'd call "movement from the interior to the exterior." 

Instead of adjusting his restrained style, Bresson elects to draw emotional flavor from the melancholy colors and sounds of the Parisian streets. As Jacques holds Marthe, the camera lingers on a bossa nova band on a bateau mouche floating through the Seine, reflecting the haunting romanticism the narrator does not express. A seeming mismatch between the text and filmmaker produces a hypnotic translation of Dostoyevsky’s dialogue-heavy work on to film.

title: Primetime (2026)
content:
The strangest scene in *Primetime* is not the hallucinatory demon vision. Somewhere around the 45 minute mark, Robert Pattinson’s Chris Hansen drags his kids out of bed to watch the latest successful taping of *To Catch a Predator*. His sons sit slack-jawed in the middle of the night as their father gloats over his new Wednesday night time slot. "Daddy’s gonna be on primetime," he seems to say, "that’s when the most people are watching\!" His kids reply with an indifferent “that’s cool.” Hansen constantly refers to his show as a righteous crusade against an evil force, but interactions like these reveal the dissonance between Hansen’s stated purpose and his warped desire for numeric validation. His identity is derived from his work, but his work is based on popularity, spectacle, and network approval.

For a film marketed around Pattinson’s portrayal of showrunner Chris Hansen, there is surprising screentime dedicated to producer Andie Bender and decoy Dan Plumb (played by Jimmy Olsen actor Skyler Gisondo). Like Hansen, these characters struggle compellingly with a career-defined identity warped by the pressure of the entertainment industry. Bender, channeling the wanton heartlessness of Faye Dunaway’s Diana in *Network*, is completely consumed by her career — her last thought after Conradt's suicide is that she can "save this." Plumb places as much stock in his job as an actor, seeking accomplishment and pride in expertise even as it alienates him and brings him to despair by the film’s ending. 

Beyond its characters, a big part of *Primetime’s* appeal is in its unique stylization. Oppenheim lends his documentary experience to creative, impeccable shot composition. The film lingers on voyeuristic close-ups of its characters framed by doorways, reflected in mirrors, and washes it all in a smoldering blue. Direct camcorder shots (screens are always REC-ording) are mixed among modern digital footage. The characters are overdramatic caricatures — Pattinson plays Hansen with intensity, dressing himself in a constructed, practiced, and gratingly inauthentic persona. In his first appearance, he recites lines back to himself before entering the set with a literal flourish through the curtains. What a diva\! *Primetime* watches less like a gritty biopic than a maddeningly entertaining fever dream.

I don’t think *Primetime* has much to offer in the way of commentary on *Predator*, or even generally on voyeurism-as-entertainment. It is, however, a gorgeous and bleakly humorous delirium accentuated by a light dose of 2000s nostalgia (who remembers *What Would You Do?*) and Pattinson’s uncanny character acting.

title: Framing and Composition in The Maltese Falcon
content:
*Originally written for LIT134: Special Studies in Film*

The characters of the Maltese Falcon hide their motives from each other, and often from themselves. Characters express themselves through lies and euphemism (the Fat Man says Wilmer is "like a son," but the audience knows he is considering betraying him). Huston formally reflects this theme through a visual emphasis on character faces. Besides a few establishing shots, the camera stays on character reactions, which Huston conceals through shadows and lighting inspired by German Expressionism. The brim of Sam Spade's hat casts a shade over his shifty eyes. O'Shaughnessy steps out unseen from a dark alleyway. When she is taken away by the police, a shadow covers her face -- is there a tear in her eye? What does she feel? The audience does not know for certain. Perhaps, in the midst of her web of deception, she does not either. 

![alt text](images/the-maltese-falcon/1.jpg "O'Shaughnessy is led away.")

All pretense is dropped for the first time when Spade and Gutman agree to sell out Wilber. The film takes an intentional moment to linger on close-up expressions of Spade, Gutman, Wilber, O'Shaughnessy, and Cairo. For the first time, the audience sees their reactions up close and unobscured. For the first time, the characters drop their facade of deception, baring their true soul.

The Maltese Falcon traps its characters in a constant struggle for control. The power dynamic constantly shifts as the characters lunge rapaciously after their own goals. The camera utilizes tight, claustrophobic framing as a reminder of this inescapable struggle. At any given time, the camera zooms in and out just enough to accommodate those displayed onscreen. Furthermore, intentional angling and composition is used to reflect volatile power dynamics. 

![alt text](images/the-maltese-falcon/2.jpg "Look at the size of that man!")

In Gutman's first conversation with Spade, he has the upper hand. The camera shoots him from an upward angle, giving him a large and domineering appearance. As the two converse, Gutman takes up a significant portion of the frame while Spade dwindles in comparison. However, the camera reminds us just how quickly this all can change. After the Fat Man is embarrassed by the revelation that his falcon is a sham, the shot changes and Spade now occupies a majority of the foreground, looking "down" onto Gutman. In a game of life, death, wit, and power, no dynamic stays stable for long.

title: Notes from Underground by Fyodor Dostoevsky
content:
When reading *Notes from Underground*, I was struck by how intimately Dostoevsky knew human ugliness. The Underground Man is absurdly, almost unbelievably pathetic. The story’s narrator — like in the pre-exile *White Nights* — is a delusional self-sabotaging dreamer who cannot separate fantasy from reality. His madness bleeds through the page as he backtracks and contradicts himself. 

Yet while *White Nights’* dreamer is hapless and almost gentle in his fantasies, the narrator of *Notes* is angrier, self-absorbed, and wholly unsympathetic. On some days, he embarks on drunken tirades before begging for forgiveness. On others, he drives himself into debt to avenge perceived slights. He is paradoxical in his ravings, longing for connection while accosting others with misanthropic rage. Nevertheless, his desire to exist as an individual remains strangely compelling through his downward spiral.

In a broader context, the novella is interesting as an ideological refutation of 19th-century Russian utilitarianism (the Man's irrational behavior challenges the utopian paradise in Chernyshevsky's *What Is to Be Done*). It’s an interesting intellectual back-and-forth told uniquely through fiction, but *Notes from Underground* stands out to me as an incisive study of the worst parts of man. Even as the Man's behavior becomes increasingly ludicrous, Dostoevsky's nuanced interior dialogue keeps his actions understandable. With every page, I was increasingly disgusted (what do you mean you walked in a circle for 3 hours to get noticed by your enemies?) and yet could never put it down.

title: How Much Land Does a Man Need?
subtitle: and Other Stories by Leo Tolstoy
content:
The short stories of Leo Tolstoy, often cited as one of the greatest writers ever, are surprisingly simple. Penguin Classic’s _How Much Land Does a Man Need & Other Stories_ collects such works, from military tales in the Caucasus to late-career didactic parables. On the surface, each short story is minimal. The prose is light and natural, characters are not over-developed, and parables have clear, obvious morals. Yet, Tolstoy’s stylistic simplicity belies an underlying profundity. War and allegory strip the characters and stories bare of pretense, accentuating enduring truths about love, death, human nature under duress, integrity, and the beauty of God’s creation.

Born into Russian nobility, Tolstoy lived an early life of privilege. After accruing severe gambling debts, Tolstoy enlisted in the army. His military experience in the mountains of the Caucasus would ignite the pacifist and humanist strain that later defined his writing. Subsequent spiritual experiences converted him into a non-violent anarchist — views which even reached a young Mahatma Gandhi. Towards the end of his career, Tolstoy focused his efforts on developing his theory of Christian anarchy. In every stage, simple plots and prose gave voice to fundamental truths.

The semi-autobiographical tales of the campaign in Chechnya feature a straightforward story structure. This intentional narrative restraint lets observations on human nature emerge. These range from ironic humor to sobering commentary, for instance on performed courage. In _The Woodfelling_, an officer “confesses” his cowardice before waiting awkwardly for the narrator to contradict him (he doesn’t). The two feign bravery moments later, uselessly sustaining a superficial conversation as death and grapeshot whizz by. Just as Tolstoy restrains his narrative structure to its core, the violence of war exposes the futility of societal civility.

Tolstoy employs an ascetic approach in his moral parables as well. In the titular _How Much Land Does a Man Need?_, an avaricious farmer makes an agreement with ethnic tribes to claim all the land he can walk around in one day. Naturally, his greed drives him farther than he can walk. The farmer pushes himself to the brink of exhaustion and returns, falling dead on the spot. His workman buries him in a six-foot grave — “exactly the right length” for him. With minimal setup and characterization, Tolstoy cuts straight to the dangers of greed. His parables are hysterically sardonic in their humor and charmingly plain in their morals.

The few times Tolstoy deserts his restrained style are to write about nature. When Tolstoy describes the mountains of the Caucasus, he paints in broad painterly strokes. Every scene is a Romantic smorgasbord of senses covered in vivid colors, hues, sights, sounds. He writes of milky-white mists, violet-grey horizons, and the mingling sounds of the night. Yet, as Tolstoy’s descriptions become more detailed, the beauty of mountains remains simple. Perhaps this serves to underline the existential contrast between nature and war. As the narrator rides through the night in _The Raid_, he wonders:
> “Can it be that there is not enough space for man in this beautiful world, under those immeasurable, starry heavens? Is it possible that man’s heart can harbor, amid such ravishing natural beauty, feelings of hatred, vengeance, or the desire to destroy his fellows? All the evil in man, one would think, should disappear in contact with Nature, the most spontaneous expression of beauty and goodness.”

Tolstoy’s short stories are pure and simple, yet wrought in profound insights and existential notes. Like he does in his longest novels, Tolstoy spots a truth of the human experience and distills it to its purest form — a few dozen pages at a time.

title: The Trial by Franz Kafka
subtitle: The absurd humor of existence
content:
I started *The Trial* having consumed some of its inescapable influence through Bulgakov's *The Master and Margarita*, Gilliam's *Brazil*, and Scorsese's *After Hours* (all personal favorites), so I had the bleak humor of navigating an absurd bureaucratic nightmare in mind as I read.

What surprised me is how subtly funny the book is. It’s not overtly ludicrous like *The* *Master and Margarita* (there are no alcoholic pistol-toting cats), and Josef K. is more outwardly subdued than Griffin Dunne’s frantic Paul Hackett. Still, the way Kafka plays ridiculous moments straight brought me to tears on the BART at least once.

One of my favorite moments is when Kafka refuses to summarize the lawyer’s lengthy monologue on the inner workings of the trial, instead making us sit through ~10 pages of legal jargon. There’s no explicit humor in the lawyer’s ramblings, but when you flip the eighth page and he’s still blathering on about inane courtroom procedure, there’s nothing you can do but laugh. Kafka gives us the experience of tedium to show the innate hilarity in K’s powerlessness.

Anyways, I wasn’t surprised to learn that Kafka was often unable to finish reading chapter drafts to his friends because he would laugh too much. For someone who wrote so vividly about alienation and existential dread, he didn’t seem to take himself too seriously. I think it’s this sense of irreverence that makes The Trial so potent as an allegory for the absurdity of life.

title: From Russia with Love (1963)
content:
**My first post!** Trying this experiment out in a dual effort to:

1. learn Claude Code and Github for my internship, and
2. document my thoughts on books, movies, and music.

Since I don't have anything prepared, I'll paste this Letterboxd review from the last movie I watched.

_From Russia with Love_ has Tintin-esque qualities — it's a flamboyant and whimsical international romp filled with quirky gadgets and larger-than-life characters, from a chess-playing spymaster to Bond's affable ally Kerim Bey. At the same time, the colorful constructed sets and vivid film stock, which create visual clarity in a way not unlike Hergé's _ligne claire_, belie a real, sinister sense of danger rooted in the Cold War tensions of the time. Terence Young blends these tones together, flipping from beautiful location shooting into visceral claustrophobic fights, then back into campy one-liners ("she's had her kicks") in a way that never feels jarring.
